node.title: Re: Parameterized Regex (updated)
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
The thing I've mainly used named captures for so far is named access to the capture groups via [doc://%+]. This can be very useful e.g. in cases like long regexes and/or if you've got one qr// regex inside another qr// regex inside another... keeping track of numbered capture groups quickly becomes impossible.

my $one = qr{ one (? \d+ ) }xi; my $two = qr{ $one two (? \d+ ) }xi; "One9Two8Three7" =~ m{ $two three (? \d+ ) }xi; use Data::Dump; dd \%+; __END__ { # tied Tie::Hash::NamedCapture one => 9, three => 7, two => 8, }

One bigger example that comes to my mind is this one: if you happen to have a 4th edition [http://shop.oreilly.com/product/9780596004927.do|Camel] (not sure if it's in the earlier ones), have a look at Chapter 5, Section "Fancy Patterns", subsection "[https://library.oreilly.com/book/9780596004927/programming-perl/225.xhtml?ref=toc|Grammatical Patterns]". You can basically build entire grammars out of them, for example using (?&NAME) you can recurse to a named subpatten ([doc://perlre]; Update: a shorter example can be found under the documentation of [doc://perlre#(DEFINE)|(DEFINE)]). Whether you want to build a full grammar using Perl's regex engine instead of one of the many well-established modules is of course another question :-)

Update 2: It seems I misread the question "What is the prevalent name for this feature" as "What is the prevalent use for this feature".

Update: Used /x and brackets to make the regexes more readable, eliminating a typo in the process. Changed the order of the paragraphs. Updated wording a little bit.
